Subject: Follow-up from demo — need packaging + savings scenarios

Hi Grace,

Thanks again for the demo yesterday — our engineering and finance leads liked the latency profile and the KV-cache story. Procurement asked me to get concrete packaging options they can take to leadership: they want to see 2–3 credible savings scenarios that show net unit economics for our primary chat workload (avg prompt 150 tokens, reply 80 tokens) and a low-latency path for peak support flows.

Quick asks:
- Can you provide 2–3 pricing scenarios that combine: batching policy, KV-prefix cache hit assumptions, and quantization level (FP16 vs int8/4-bit variants)?
- Any recommended guardrails where accuracy drops meaningfully with quant? (we care about NER/slot extraction)
- A short attachment with the savings math and a formal quote we can pass to procurement would be ideal.

We'd like to review this week if possible — can you circle back by EOD Friday PST?

Thanks,
Sara

Head of Integrations, Nimble Shop

Hi Sara — thanks for the clear asks and glad the demo was useful. Attached is a working sheet (nimble_savings_model_v3.xlsx) and a draft quote (redwood_quote_nimble_v2.pdf). Summary below — I'll outline three scenarios and the assumptions so procurement can compare side-by-side.

Executive summary (tl;dr):
- Scenario A (Conservative): FP16 model, modest batching (max batch 8), KV-cache with 20% effective prefix hit on repetitive prompts. Estimated ~22% token-cost reduction vs naive per-request baseline.
- Scenario B (Balanced): int8 quantization (weight-only), batching tuned to 16 tokens/session windows, KV-cache 35% hit. Estimated ~41% token-cost reduction and modest latency improvement for tail p95.
- Scenario C (Aggressive Efficiency): 4-bit quant + asymmetric quant kernels (recommended for non-critical LLM ops), aggressive batching (dynamic batching up to 24 with adaptive timeouts), KV-cache 50% on common prefixes. Estimated ~58% token-cost reduction but requires evaluation on NER accuracy and a short A/B safety check.

Notes on accuracy:
- For NER/slot extraction we typically see <1.5% delta FP16 -> int8 on curated prompt sets, but 4-bit requires a 2–4% validation pass on your representative prompt set. We'll run a quick eval on your sample prompts if you send them.

Operational notes:
- We recommend starting with Scenario B for production pilot; it balances cost and accuracy and allows a canary to fail back to FP16 automatically (we'll include a rollout policy in the quote).
- KV-cache sizing: we modeled average prefix length 40 tokens; cache hit assumptions in the spreadsheet are adjustable.
- Batching: for support flows where p95 latency matters, we propose an autoscaling policy that prioritizes low-latency routes and routes them to a small dedicated pool. See 'route' rows in the sheet.

Next steps I propose:
1) We run a 2-week evaluation with Scenario B (we'll credit 4,000,000 tokens during the pilot).
2) We run a quick NER accuracy check for your sample 250 prompts (you to share).
3) Procurement and legal sign off on quote/PO — I included two term options in the PDF.

I'm leaving for a customer offsite Thursday afternoon; Connor and Monica are looped to finalize the quote and evaluate the 4-bit impact if you want to explore Scenario C after the pilot.

Attachments: nimble_savings_model_v3.xlsx (spreadsheet), redwood_quote_nimble_v2.pdf (pdf)

Thanks — Grace

Quick technical clarifications to support the spreadsheet assumptions:

- Quant recommendations: For your workload (heavy slot-filling, occasional long context), int8 weight-only quantization gives the best cost/accuracy compromise across our benchmarks. For 4-bit we recommend per-layer calibration with asymmetric quant kernels; it's powerful for embeddings and forward-only servers but introduces small churn in conditional generation, so we'll gate it behind the eval.
- Cache semantics: we assumed prefix-KV caching that stores decoder KV states for the last 6 user-turns per conversation; this increases hit for multi-turn flows but requires ~6–10MB per active conversation depending on sequence length. Sheet models memory overheads.
- Batching policy: the cost math in the sheet uses a hybrid continuous-batching model — requests are batched opportunistically for short windows (25ms) and we allow occasional flushes for latency-sensitive routes. If Nimble wants more aggressive batching we can add jittering to align requests and push efficiency up ~8–12% but that raises p95 by 30–80ms depending on traffic shape.

I'll run a quick micro-benchmark against your sample if you share 50 representative sessions; that will let us replace modeled numbers with empirical p95/p99 deltas.

-Karthik
Karthik Iyer
Lead Systems Architect, Redwood Inference
